title: Alec Guinness
wiki_lead:
Sir Alec Guinness (born Alec Guinness de Cuffe; 2 April 1914 – 5 August 2000) was an English actor. He is widely acclaimed as one of the most important stage and film actors of the 20th Century. In the BFI listing of the 100 most important British films of the 20th century, he was the single most noted actor. Guiness appeared in nine films across the list, six in starring roles and three in supporting roles, including five films directed by David Lean and four from Ealing Studios. His accolades include an Academy Award, a BAFTA, a Golden Globe, a Tony Award and a Volpi Cup. In 1959, he was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II for services to the arts. He received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 1960, the Academy Honorary Award for lifetime achievement in 1980 and the BAFTA Academy Fellowship Award in 1989.
Guinness began his stage career in 1934. Two years later, at the age of 22, he played the role of Osric in Hamlet in the West End and joined the Old Vic. He continued to play Shakespearean roles throughout his career. He served in the Royal Naval Reserve during the Second World War and commanded a landing craft during the invasion of Sicily and Elba. Along with Laurence Olivier, John Gielgud and Ralph Richardson, he was one of the great British theatre actors who made the transition to films after the war, making his name in six Ealing comedies, starting in 1949 with both A Run for Your Money and Kind Hearts and Coronets (in which he played eight different characters). He went on to lead roles in 1951 with The Man in the White Suit and The Lavender Hill Mob (for which he received his first Academy Award nomination for Best Actor), then in 1955 with The Ladykillers, and culminating in 1957 with Barnacle Bill. 
Guinness collaborated six times with director David Lean: as Herbert Pocket in Great Expectations (1946); Fagin in Oliver Twist (1948); Col. Nicholson in The Bridge on the River Kwai (1957), for which he won both the Academy Award and the BAFTA Award for Best Actor; Prince Faisal in Lawrence of Arabia (1962); General Yevgraf Zhivago in Doctor Zhivago (1965); and Professor Godbole in A Passage to India (1984). In 1970, Guinness played Jacob Marley's ghost in Ronald Neame's Scrooge. He also portrayed Obi-Wan Kenobi in George Lucas's original Star Wars trilogy, which brought him further recognition. For his performance in the original 1977 film, Guinness was nominated as Best Supporting Actor for the Academy Award and Golden Globe. Guinness's later life was also associated with his definitive depiction of the leading role of George Smiley in the BBC television series Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy and Smiley's People by John le Carré.

grok_lead: Sir Alec Guinness (2 April 1914 â 5 August 2000) was an English actor celebrated for his extraordinary versatility, portraying a wide array of characters across stage and screen over a career spanning more than six decades. Born in Maida Vale, London, to an unmarried mother, Guinness pursued acting after modest beginnings in advertising and training at the Fay Compton Studio of Dramatic Art. Guinness first gained prominence on the stage in the 1930s, joining the Old Vic company and performing in productions like Hamlet and Richard III, before transitioning to film with his debut as Herbert Pocket in David Lean's Great Expectations (1946). He became a star of British cinema in the post-war era, excelling in Ealing Studios comedies such as Kind Hearts and Coronets (1949), where he played eight different roles, and The Lavender Hill Mob (1951). His dramatic range shone in roles like Colonel Nicholson in The Bridge on the River Kwai (1957), earning him the Academy Award for Best Actor, and Fagin in Oliver Twist (1948). Later in his career, Guinness achieved international fame as Obi-Wan Kenobi in the Star Wars trilogy (1977â1983), though he expressed ambivalence toward the role and its cultural impact. He also delivered acclaimed television performances, notably as the introspective spy George Smiley in adaptations of John le CarrÃ©'s novels, including Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy (1979). Knighted in 1959 and appointed a Companion of Honour in 1994, Guinness received multiple honors, including a Tony Award in 1964 and an honorary Academy Award in 1980 for his contributions to film. In his personal life, he married actress Merula Salaman in 1938, with whom he had one son, Matthew, and converted to Roman Catholicism in 1956; the couple remained together until his death from liver cancer in Midhurst, West Sussex.
